questions.question: Define migration and distinguish it from circulation, then classify population movements along the three axes used by geographers, giving an example of each type.
questions.expected_answer: Migration is a permanent or semi-permanent change of a person's place of residence. Circulation covers repeated temporary movements that always return home without changing residence — daily commuting, learners boarding at school, seasonal farm workers following harvests. True migration is classified along three axes. By place: internal migration occurs within one country, such as moving from the rural Eastern Cape to Gauteng, with the mover an out-migrant at the origin and in-migrant at the destination; international migration crosses a border, the mover being an emigrant from the country left and an immigrant into the country entered. Internal streams include rural-urban, the dominant stream in developing countries driving urbanisation, plus urban-rural, rural-rural and urban-urban. By choice: voluntary migration is chosen, usually for work or education; forced migration leaves no reasonable choice — refugees have crossed a border fleeing persecution or conflict, asylum seekers await recognition of that status, and internally displaced persons flee within their own country; apartheid-era forced removals from District Six and Sophiatown are South African examples of forced internal movement. By duration: permanent migration intends no return, while temporary migration includes the circular or oscillating pattern of the historical mine contract system — eleven months on the mines and December at home, repeated for years.

questions.question: Explain the push-pull model of migration, including the four families of factors, the obstacles between origin and destination, and the role of perception.
questions.expected_answer: Push factors are the negatives of the origin that drive people out; pull factors are the attractions of the destination that draw them in, and every migration should be explained with both. The four families are: economic — unemployment, low wages and failing farms push, while jobs, higher wages and a city's economy pull, and economic factors dominate world migration; social — poor schools and distant clinics push, while good schools, hospitals, services and family already settled pull, with established migrant communities easing each next move in chain migration; political — war, persecution and instability push, peace and safety pull; environmental — drought, floods and exhausted soils push, reliable rain and productive land pull. The decision weighs these against intervening obstacles — the cost of the journey, distance, borders and permits, and the wrench of leaving family — so migration happens only when perceived gain outweighs perceived cost. Perception matters because migrants move on the picture of the destination in their heads, formed by relatives' stories and social media, which is often brighter than reality; this gap explains why migration continues into cities that already suffer severe unemployment.

questions.question: Discuss the migration stream from the rural Eastern Cape to Gauteng and the international stream into South Africa, explaining causes and evaluating consequences for both origin and destination areas.
questions.expected_answer: The Eastern Cape stream has historical roots: the homeland system confined the majority population to poor land in areas such as the former Transkei and Ciskei, while the migrant labour system sent men on mine contracts to the Witwatersrand under pass laws that barred their families; when controls ended in the 1990s, families could move together. Pushes include rural unemployment, tiny overworked plots and thin services; pulls include Gauteng's concentration of jobs, better schools and hospitals, and established home-community networks. The origin gains remittances and returning skills but loses working-age adults, leaving villages of children and grandparents, uncultivated fields and a hollowed age structure; the destination gains a young workforce but faces informal settlement growth, overcrowded services and job competition. Many migrants remain circular, keeping a rural home and remitting monthly. Internationally, the largest stream flows from Zimbabwe following its economic collapse from around 2000 — hyperinflation, unemployment and political fear pushing, while South Africa's economy, shared border and networks pull; the flow is mixed migration, containing economic migrants, refugees and asylum seekers, joining older streams of Mozambican and Basotho mineworkers and refugees from the DRC, Somalia and Ethiopia. Origin countries gain lifeline remittances but suffer a brain drain of teachers and nurses; South Africa gains labour, businesses and scarce skills but experiences pressure on housing, services and low-end jobs, which has ignited xenophobic violence, notably in 2008 and 2015, at heavy human cost.
